A 2-day history of right ring finger swelling and pain after mechanical trauma (jersey entanglement). Exam shows DIP joint–localized swelling, tenderness, and active flexion deficit — but no confirmed Kanavel’s signs, no skin breach, no systemic features, and no radiographic bony abnormality. X-ray confirms soft tissue swelling; MRI is indicated and underway but unreported. Ultrasound, CBC, CRP/ESR, and wound culture remain pending. Differential includes:  
- Septic DIP arthritis,  
- Early or localized flexor tenosynovitis (despite lack of classic signs),

- Post-traumatic inflammatory arthropathy or reactive synovitis.

Obtain and interpret the **MRI report**, with specific attention to:  
- Fluid/enhancement within the flexor tendon sheath (tenosynovitis),

[THOUGHT]  
The case describes a 2-day post-traumatic right ring finger DIP joint–localized swelling and pain following jersey entanglement — a classic mechanism for forced hyperextension or avulsion injury. Key clinical features include: (1) isolated DIP swelling/tenderness, (2) active flexion deficit (i.e., inability to actively bend the DIP joint), (3) absence of Kanavel’s signs (so no classic flexor tenosynovitis), (4) no skin breach or systemic signs, and (5) normal X-ray excluding fracture or dislocation but confirming soft tissue swelling. The active flexion deficit is highly specific: in the ring finger, isolated loss of active DIP flexion — especially after trauma — strongly suggests disruption of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon, most commonly an avulsion from its distal insertion at the volar base of the distal phalanx (i.e., “jersey finger”). This diagnosis explains the DIP-localized findings, preserved passive motion (implied by absence of passive-extension pain or description of passive restriction), lack of inflammatory systemic signs, and normal bony imaging (avulsion fractures may be radiographically occult but are often subtle or non-displaced; MRI would show tendon retraction and bone marrow edema at the insertion). While septic arthritis and tenosynovitis remain in the differential, they are less likely given the absence of warmth, erythema, fever, Kanavel’s signs, or lab evidence of inflammation — and crucially, because active flexion deficit without concomitant passive extension pain or fusiform swelling makes infection less probable. Reactive synovitis or traumatic arthropathy would not typically cause isolated active flexion loss. MRI — though pending — is expected to reveal FDP tendon discontinuity/retraction and possibly a small avulsion fragment or marrow edema at the volar distal phalanx — findings diagnostic of jersey finger.

- Mechanism: Jersey entanglement — classic cause of forced DIP hyperextension and FDP avulsion.

- Active flexion deficit at the DIP joint — hallmark of FDP dysfunction.

Diagnostician:

[THOUGHT]  
The case describes a 2-day post-traumatic right ring finger DIP joint–localized swelling and pain following jersey entanglement — a classic mechanism for forced hyperextension or avulsion injury. Key clinical features include: (1) isolated DIP swelling/tenderness, (2) active flexion deficit (i.e., inability to actively bend the DIP joint), (3) absence of Kanavel’s signs (so no classic flexor tenosynovitis), (4) no skin breach or systemic signs, and (5) normal X-ray excluding fracture or dislocation but confirming soft tissue swelling. The active flexion deficit is highly specific: in the ring finger, isolated loss of active DIP flexion — especially after trauma — strongly suggests disruption of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon, most commonly an avulsion from its distal insertion at the volar base of the distal phalanx (i.e., “jersey finger”). This diagnosis explains the DIP-localized findings, preserved passive motion (implied by absence of passive-extension pain or description of passive restriction), lack of inflammatory systemic signs, and normal bony imaging (avulsion fractures may be radiographically occult but are often subtle or non-displaced; MRI would show tendon retraction and bone marrow edema at the insertion). While septic arthritis and tenosynovitis remain in the differential, they are less likely given the absence of warmth, erythema, fever, Kanavel’s signs, or lab evidence of inflammation — and crucially, because active flexion deficit without concomitant passive extension pain or fusiform swelling makes infection less probable. Reactive synovitis or traumatic arthropathy would not typically cause isolated active flexion loss. MRI — though pending — is expected to reveal FDP tendon discontinuity/retraction and possibly a small avulsion fragment or marrow edema at the volar distal phalanx — findings diagnostic of jersey finger.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Mechanism: Jersey entanglement — classic cause of forced DIP hyperextension and FDP avulsion.  
- Isolated DIP joint–localized swelling and tenderness — consistent with distal tendon or insertion injury.  
- Active flexion deficit at the DIP joint — hallmark of FDP dysfunction.  
- No confirmed Kanavel’s signs — argues against flexor tenosynovitis.  
- No skin breach — lowers likelihood of inoculation-driven septic arthritis/tenosynovitis.  
- No systemic features (e.g., fever, chills) — reduces suspicion for infection.  
- Normal X-ray with only soft tissue swelling — typical for radiographically occult FDP avulsion (up to 25% lack visible bony fragment).  
- Traumatic onset over 2 days — aligns with acute tendon injury rather than insidious inflammatory process.

[GAPS]  
- MRI report — specifically whether it shows FDP tendon discontinuity, retraction, or avulsion fragment at the distal phalanx insertion.  
- Physical exam detail on passive DIP flexion/extension — to confirm preservation of passive motion (expected in jersey finger, lost in tenosynovitis or joint sepsis).  
- Presence/absence of volar tenderness at the DIP flexion crease — a key localizing sign for FDP avulsion.  
- Ultrasound result — could demonstrate tendon gap or retraction if performed expertly.  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Jersey finger (flexor digitorum profundus avulsion injury)
